claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase, continuous lamellar colonies.
The numerous internal boundaries in the lamellar colonies serve as room-temperature tensile microcrack-initiation sites.
A brief anneal near the eutectic temperature will partially disrupt lamellar continuity.
The proposed anneal will cause moderate spheroidization at interphase boundaries.
The proposed anneal and quench will produce hierarchical subgrain structures.
Near-eutectic annealing provides enough atomic mobility to relax and rearrange interlamellar boundaries.
Near-eutectic annealing reduces boundary continuity and smooths sharp geometric features.
Rapid quenching preserves the anneal-induced microstructural changes.
Partial lamellar disruption and boundary smoothing reduce local stress concentrations and crack-initiation sites.
The treated alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated lamellar baseline.
The treated alloy will maintain or improve yield strength relative to the untreated lamellar baseline.
The treated alloy will maintain or improve ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated lamellar baseline.
The intervention is effective only within a temperature-time window that causes partial rather than complete disruption of lamellar continuity.
Temperatures outside near-eutectic conditions or insufficient quench rates may prevent the desired refinement and limit efficacy.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility changes may depend on alloy composition and processing parameters.
Residual stresses and other microstructural features may influence the response to treatment.
SEM/TEM characterization and room-temperature tensile testing of treated and untreated samples can test the predicted mediator and mechanical outcomes.
